borders.before: the lecture's introductory framing, overview of the lecture series, and stated learning objectives
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease with complex microenvironmental interactions
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is pure administrative and lecture framing, whereas subtopic 2 begins the substantive subject matter of the lecture by asking what cancer is fundamentally.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no basis for moving it; subtopic 1 contains only syllabus and objective setup, while subtopic 2 introduces the biological definition.
borders.caseForRemoving: The opening framing is distinct from the substantive conceptual teaching that begins at subtopic 2.

borders.before: broad epidemiological patterns and geographical variations in cancer incidence across international populations
borders.after: specific biological and infectious pathogens that act as cancer-causing agents
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 6 finishes the macro-level demographic and epidemiological framing, while subtopic 7 shifts to evaluating individual carcinogenic agents and their biological mechanisms starting with infectious pathogens.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving to subtopic 8 would orphan the general introduction to oncogenic pathogens in subtopic 7; moving to subtopic 6 would merge general epidemiology with specific causal agent analysis.
borders.caseForRemoving: The high-level statistical and epidemiological overview in subtopics 2–6 answers whether cancer is caused by genetics or environment, whereas subtopic 7 onwards examines specific carcinogenic mechanisms.

borders.before: chemical carcinogens in cigarette smoke and tissue-specific enzymatic metabolic activation in the bladder
borders.after: non-mutagenic carcinogens like asbestos and the concept of cancer promotion versus initiation
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 14 introduces a fundamental mechanistic shift from direct DNA-damaging mutagens (initiators) to non-mutagenic agents that drive cancer via chronic inflammation and microenvironmental promotion.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 13 is strictly about chemical activation of beta-naphthylamine, so the boundary sits exactly where asbestos is introduced to demonstrate non-mutagenic promotion in 14.
borders.caseForRemoving: Direct mutational adduct formation (subtopics 9–13) is conceptually distinct from the two-stage initiation-promotion paradigm and host tissue susceptibility introduced in 14–17.

borders.before: a synthesis summarizing mechanisms of DNA damage, direct versus indirect actions, promoters, and host susceptibility
borders.after: experimental and analytical methods for identifying carcinogens, starting with mutational signature profiling from whole genome sequencing
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 17 concludes the mechanistic exploration of carcinogenesis, and subtopic 18 begins a new section focused on the investigative methodologies used to identify and prove carcinogenicity.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 17 is a clear summary of the preceding mechanistic concepts and belongs with them; moving the border to 17 would inappropriately start the methodologies topic with a recap of biological mechanisms.
borders.caseForRemoving: Explaining the biological mechanisms of how cancer develops is distinct from evaluating the toxicological and genomic methodologies used to prove an exposure is carcinogenic.

borders.before: the Ames test and in vitro toxicological assays used to test mutagenicity
borders.after: closing synthesis, risk-benefit decision-making considerations, and concluding remarks
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 21 ends the review of experimental methodologies, whereas subtopic 22 provides the closing synthesis and parting perspective on real-world risk-benefit balancing.
borders.caseForMoving: Subtopic 21 is a specific in vitro methodology (Ames test) and belongs with the methods topic; subtopic 22 is purely concluding wrap-up.
borders.caseForRemoving: The final summary and closing reflection on everyday risk assessment represents the standard closing framing of the lecture.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2–4 discuss the fundamental nature of cancer and specific mutagenic exposures, while subtopics 5–6 focus on the scientific and public debate regarding random bad luck versus epidemiology.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2–6 together form a single introductory framework addressing the balance between intrinsic random mutation ('bad luck') and external environmental exposures supported by global epidemiological trends.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7–8 deal exclusively with infectious pathogens (viruses, bacteria, parasites), whereas subtopics 9–13 examine dietary toxins, radiation, and xenobiotic chemical mutagens.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 7–13 represent a continuous progression of specific direct carcinogenic agents and their molecular mechanisms of inducing DNA damage and adduct formation.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 14–15 explain the initiation versus promotion paradigm (asbestos, DMBA/TPA), while subtopics 16–17 explore host developmental timing, life-stage susceptibility, and a summarizing recap.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: The entire group addresses factors beyond direct mutational initiation—specifically how inflammatory promoters, tissue contexts, and host developmental states enable clonal outgrowth, summarized together in subtopic 17.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 18–19 focus on human-based retrospective methods (mutational signatures and biobank epidemiology), while subtopics 20–21 focus on experimental laboratory models (in vivo animal studies and the Ames test).
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18–21 systematically walk through the complementary suite of methodologies (genomics, epidemiology, animal models, in vitro assays) used to determine and prove carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Lecture Introduction and Learning Objectives
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer introduces herself, outlines the cancer lecture series, and sets out the core learning objectives.

topics.label: Origins, Drivers, and Epidemiological Evidence of Cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish cancer as an evolutionary genetic disease influenced by a balance of intrinsic biological errors, genetic predisposition, and environmental exposures evidenced by epidemiological data.

topics.label: Mechanisms of Pathogen, Chemical, and Physical Carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain the specific molecular mechanisms by which infectious agents, dietary compounds, radiation, and metabolized chemical toxins damage DNA and drive oncogenesis.

topics.label: Tumor Initiation, Promotion, and Host Susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore non-mutagenic promotional mechanisms, the initiation-promotion paradigm, and host developmental and tissue-specific factors that govern cancer emergence.

topics.label: Methodologies for Assessing and Proving Carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics evaluate the genomic, epidemiological, in vivo, and in vitro experimental strategies used to detect carcinogens and establish their causal link to cancer.

topics.label: Summary and Risk-Benefit Analysis
topics.groupedBecause: The lecturer concludes the session with a recap of key concepts and frames cancer risk within practical daily risk-benefit decision-making.
